ideas.title: Encryption in Data Transmission
ideas.learningGap: Learners can repeat that encryption keeps data safe but may not connect that claim to the observable difference between plaintext and ciphertext on a shared transmission path, or to the exact key action that lets the intended receiver recover the message.
ideas.overlapCheck: The current catalogue has no encryption lab. Parity & ARQ models transmission errors and retries, while Network Topology and CSMA/CD model routing or contention; none hide message content or teach symmetric/asymmetric key use. The three immutable reference labs also contain no encryption interaction.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the need for and purpose of encryption when transmitting data
Understand how data is encrypted using symmetric and asymmetric encryption

references.title: OpenLearn: the key distribution problem
references.teachingConnection: Frames the practical problem of sharing a symmetric secret over a watched channel.

references.title: Public Key Cryptography Interactivity | NRICH
references.teachingConnection: Makes Alice, Bob, Eve and key-role consequences concrete.

references.title: Public Key Cryptography - Computerphile
references.teachingConnection: The Computerphile video explains public/private key cryptography through a concrete communication analogy. It is useful inspiration for a visually legible message journey and role separation, not for reproducing its media or implementation.

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science 0478/11 Paper 1 May/Jun 2024
references.teachingConnection: The official paper asks learners to place plain text, cipher text, public key, and private key in an asymmetric-transmission sequence. This anchors the interaction vocabulary and intended exam-level outcome.

interaction.learnerAction: Learner sends a short message through a channel after choosing either no encryption, a shared symmetric key, or the receiver's public/private key route.
interaction.visibleChange: An eavesdropper panel shows readable plaintext on the open route, ciphertext on encrypted routes, and whether the receiver can recover the message with the selected key; a wrong key leaves the message locked.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Encryption protects data in transit by transforming plaintext into ciphertext. Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key at both ends, while asymmetric encryption uses the receiver's public key to encrypt and private key to decrypt.

ideas.revisedDirection: One secure-communications workbench: operate key chips, encryptor/decryptor sockets, a watched link and retained captured traffic. Shared-key handoff and public/private roles belong inside this one system.
ideas.distinctGap: It teaches confidentiality and endpoint key actions; Parity/ARQ teaches corrupted-frame detection and retransmission, while the network labs teach movement and contention.

assessment.summary: The syllabus outcome, official assessment vocabulary, NRICH role model and Computerphile explanation converge on one inspectable transmission. The learner can compare readable plaintext, ciphertext and successful key use without implementing cryptographic mathematics or a network simulator.

ideas.title: Symmetric Key Distribution
ideas.learningGap: Learners may know that symmetric encryption uses one key but fail to see why a sender and receiver who have not already shared that secret cannot safely send the key across a channel monitored by an eavesdropper.
ideas.overlapCheck: No existing lab models key distribution. Parity & ARQ exposes corruption and retransmission, not confidentiality or a stolen key; the reference labs do not cover encryption. This is related to the eavesdropper idea but focuses narrowly on the setup problem rather than message readability alone.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the need for and purpose of encryption when transmitting data
Understand how data is encrypted using symmetric and asymmetric encryption

references.title: NRICH Public Key Cryptography
references.teachingConnection: Makes Alice, Bob, Eve and key-role consequences concrete.

references.title: The Key Distribution Problem | OpenLearn, The Open University
references.teachingConnection: Frames the practical problem of sharing a symmetric secret over a watched channel.

references.title: Public key encryption | Khan Academy
references.teachingConnection: Khan Academy frames the learner's practical question: how can two computers exchange a shared symmetric key when an attacker can watch the wire? Its contrast between a shared key and public-key encryption supports a focused key-handoff puzzle.

references.title: Public Key Cryptography - Computerphile
references.teachingConnection: The video supplies a memorable public/private-key analogy that can motivate why a public key may travel openly while the private key remains with the receiver. Use only the conceptual inspiration; do not reproduce its presentation or assets.

interaction.learnerAction: Learner first sends a symmetric key openly, then reruns the same message setup using a receiver's public key to protect the secret key before sending the message.
interaction.visibleChange: Eve copies the openly sent symmetric key and can unlock subsequent ciphertext; in the second run Eve sees a public key and wrapped key but the receiver's private-key step alone reveals the shared secret.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Symmetric encryption can protect the message once both sides share a secret, but sending that secret openly defeats the protection. Asymmetric public/private keys provide a way to protect the handoff.

ideas.revisedDirection: Fold into the encryption workbench as a counterfactual: openly send the shared key, then protect that handoff with the receiver's public key.
ideas.distinctGap: It isolates secure establishment of a shared secret, an outcome not present in any current transmission, stack or memory lab.

assessment.summary: The Open University Alice/Bob/Eve sequence supports a sharp causal realization: sending a shared secret openly lets Eve decrypt later traffic. However, key distribution is an inferred extension of the cited 0478 wording and substantially overlaps the broader encryption-transmission candidate.

ideas.title: Public and Private Key Roles
ideas.learningGap: Learners often reverse public and private key roles or treat the two keys as interchangeable, especially when describing which key encrypts a private message for a named receiver.
ideas.overlapCheck: There is no key-role or encryption lab in the current catalogue. Existing transmission labs use packet state, error flags, and routing decisions; they do not ask which key acts at each endpoint. This is narrower than the shared-key handoff and could become a short diagnostic rather than a full simulation.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the need for and purpose of encryption when transmitting data
Understand how data is encrypted using symmetric and asymmetric encryption

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science 0478/11 Paper 1 May/Jun 2024
references.teachingConnection: The official question tests the ordered relationship from plain text to cipher text using a public key, then decryption using a private key. It identifies a precise role confusion worth diagnosing interactively.

references.title: Public Key Cryptography Interactivity | NRICH
references.teachingConnection: Makes Alice, Bob, Eve and key-role consequences concrete.

interaction.learnerAction: Learner assigns the available key cards to the encrypt and decrypt steps for a message addressed to Bob, then attempts the transmission.
interaction.visibleChange: Only the route using Bob's public key for encryption and Bob's private key for decryption reaches readable text; misplaced keys produce an explicit locked or failed receiver state.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: For asymmetric encryption, the receiver's public key can be shared and is used to encrypt a message to that receiver; the matching private key is kept secret and decrypts it.

ideas.revisedDirection: Use as a diagnostic condition inside encryption, not a standalone key-matching activity.
ideas.distinctGap: It targets reversal of the receiver's public-encrypt/private-decrypt roles, which no existing lab addresses.

assessment.summary: The misconception and official evidence are strong, but assigning key cards may remain a decorated recall exercise. It also sits inside the richer consequence already available in the encryption-eavesdropper candidate.

ideas.title: Hybrid Symmetric and Asymmetric Encryption
ideas.learningGap: Learners may see symmetric and asymmetric encryption as competing alternatives and miss the useful division in which asymmetric encryption protects a small shared key while symmetric encryption handles the message itself.
ideas.overlapCheck: No catalogue lab combines two encryption abstractions, and no current lab covers key setup. This is distinct from the basic public/private route but extends beyond the literal 0478 wording, so it must not become a TLS, certificate, or performance simulation.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the need for and purpose of encryption when transmitting data
Understand how data is encrypted using symmetric and asymmetric encryption

references.title: OpenLearn: the key distribution problem
references.teachingConnection: Frames the practical problem of sharing a symmetric secret over a watched channel.

references.title: Teach teens computing: Encryption and cryptography | Raspberry Pi Foundation
references.teachingConnection: The Raspberry Pi Foundation course targets ages 14-16, compares symmetric and asymmetric schemes, and explicitly includes a module on the two working together. That provides a concrete teaching reference while the proposed lab uses an original two-envelope abstraction.

references.title: 0478 Unit 2: Data transmission and encryption | PG Online
references.teachingConnection: This 0478-specific unit isolates encryption as its final lesson and states that learners demonstrate both asymmetric and symmetric encryption. It supports curriculum fit, but does not justify adding a broad protocol or HTTPS simulator.

interaction.learnerAction: Learner sends a long message by choosing whether to wrap a short symmetric session key with the receiver's public key before using that session key for the message.
interaction.visibleChange: The channel shows a small protected key envelope followed by one consistent symmetric ciphertext stream; removing the envelope leaves the receiver without the key, while Eve still sees only ciphertext.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The two methods can serve different roles: asymmetric public/private encryption protects key delivery, and symmetric encryption uses the shared key to protect the larger transmitted message.

ideas.revisedDirection: The curriculum concept may support a worthwhile lab, but the current interaction hypothesis still needs a stronger causal centre before automation.
ideas.distinctGap: It teaches complementary roles for asymmetric key delivery and symmetric message protection, absent from the current catalogue.

assessment.summary: The envelope model is concrete and well referenced, but the combined modern scheme and implied performance rationale extend beyond the literal 0478 outcome. It risks adding a second cryptographic mechanism before the core distinction is secure.

ideas.title: Small-Key RSA and Security Limits
ideas.learningGap: Learners may assume that any scrambled output is secure and may not distinguish demonstrating encryption/decryption from demonstrating resistance to an attacker; a tiny public-key example can expose that difference.
ideas.overlapCheck: No current lab teaches encryption strength or key attacks. The idea does not overlap existing labs, but it is less directly required by 0478 section 2.3 than the purpose and key-role candidates and risks turning into an RSA mathematics lesson.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the need for and purpose of encryption when transmitting data
Understand how data is encrypted using symmetric and asymmetric encryption

references.title: RSA Interactive | Maths Is Fun
references.teachingConnection: Useful only when small-number RSA mathematics is the intended object.

references.title: Teach teens computing: Encryption and cryptography | Raspberry Pi Foundation
references.teachingConnection: The course places simple ciphers and modern symmetric/asymmetric encryption in an age-14-to-16 teaching sequence. That supports a possible bridge from visible scrambling to modern key-based encryption, but section 2.3 itself does not require RSA arithmetic.

interaction.learnerAction: Learner encrypts a short message with a deliberately tiny public-key example, then asks the built-in eavesdropper to attempt recovery by factoring the visible modulus.
interaction.visibleChange: The receiver decrypts with the private key immediately, while the eavesdropper can also recover the message only when the toy modulus is small; a larger abstract key shows the attack becoming impractical without simulating real cryptography.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Encryption changes plaintext into ciphertext using keys, but a teaching toy is not automatically secure. Key size and the difficulty of deriving a private key matter, although RSA mathematics is outside the core 0478 section 2.3 requirement.

ideas.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
ideas.distinctGap: It distinguishes reversible scrambling from practical security, a concept absent from current labs but not explicitly required by the cited syllabus.

assessment.summary: The toy attack exposes an important misconception, but RSA factorisation and key strength are outside the core requirement and could pull attention toward mathematics rather than the purpose and roles of encryption.

ideas.title: Internet and World Wide Web
ideas.learningGap: Learners often use Internet and World Wide Web interchangeably, so the dependency between Internet infrastructure and the Web service remains an abstract definition.
ideas.overlapCheck: Closest existing labs are network-topology (packet movement through a network) and software-stack (a generic browser application tile). Neither distinguishes Internet infrastructure from the Web's browser, HTTP and HTML service.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the difference between the internet and the world wide web

references.title: MDN: how the web works
references.teachingConnection: Grounds the request sequence without prescribing a lab shell.

references.title: World Wide Web - MDN Glossary
references.teachingConnection: MDN explicitly states that the Web is a system of public web pages built on the Internet and lists HTTP, URLs and HTML as its components; this supports an original two-layer dependency model without copying its analogy or design.

references.title: How does the Internet work? - MDN
references.teachingConnection: The article contrasts the Internet as technical infrastructure with the Web as a service and notes that email is another service, giving a concrete non-Web comparison for a restrained classification task.

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science 0478 | Internet & WWW - YouTube
references.teachingConnection: The syllabus-focused lesson covers Internet versus WWW alongside browser, URL and retrieval terms; it is useful as a coverage check, not as a visual or script source.

interaction.learnerAction: Place cards for Internet infrastructure, browser, HTTP, HTML page and email into an Internet layer and a Web-service layer, then remove the Internet layer.
interaction.visibleChange: The Web page lane stops when its infrastructure layer is removed, while the email service remains labelled as a different Internet service; misplaced cards receive local feedback.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The Internet is the underlying infrastructure; the World Wide Web is one service of linked pages and protocols that uses that infrastructure.

ideas.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
ideas.distinctGap: It separates infrastructure from one service, whereas Network Topology teaches packet movement and Software Stack only depicts a browser application.

assessment.summary: The misconception is syllabus-relevant, but the proposed card placement and layer removal remain close to a terminology sort. The email contrast helps, yet the visible consequence is largely definitional rather than an independently explorable mechanism.

ideas.title: URL Structure and Resource Location
ideas.learningGap: Learners can repeat that a URL is a web address but may not connect its protocol, domain and page/file name to the request made by a browser.
ideas.overlapCheck: Closest existing lab is software-stack, where a browser appears only as generic application content. No existing lab lets a learner change URL parts and observe a different protocol, server or resource target.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand what is meant by a uniform resource locator (URL)

references.title: NetLab packet-path simulator
references.teachingConnection: Shows a bounded DNS/ARP/TCP/TLS journey through inspectable network steps.

references.title: What is a URL? - MDN
references.teachingConnection: Connects URL components to the resource a request targets.

references.title: How the Internet Works - STEM Explorer
references.teachingConnection: This interactive starts with URL parsing and shows protocol, domain and path before DNS and HTTP, providing a concrete interaction reference while the new lab can reduce the model to the syllabus's essential fields.

interaction.learnerAction: Assemble one fictional URL by choosing its protocol, domain and page/file name, then change only one part before pressing Request.
interaction.visibleChange: The request card highlights the selected protocol, server and resource; changing the domain or file name changes the destination/result while the other fields stay fixed.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A URL is structured text that tells the browser how to communicate, which domain's server to contact and which page or file to request.

ideas.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
ideas.distinctGap: It makes individual URL fields causally determine protocol, server and resource, which existing networking labs do not show.

assessment.summary: Changing one URL component and holding the others fixed is a restrained causal interaction. Evidence is adequate, but the concept may be more efficiently taught as a stage inside the stronger URL-to-page retrieval candidate.

ideas.title: DNS and Web Page Retrieval
ideas.learningGap: Learners often memorize browser, DNS, IP, server and HTML as a list without seeing why the browser must resolve a domain before it can request and display a page.
ideas.overlapCheck: Closest existing labs are network-topology (generic packet routing) and software-stack (generic browser app). Neither models the distinct web retrieval chain from URL through DNS/IP and web server to returned HTML.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Describe how web pages are located, retrieved and displayed on a device when a user enters a URL

references.title: NetLab packet-path simulator
references.teachingConnection: Shows a bounded DNS/ARP/TCP/TLS journey through inspectable network steps.

references.title: How the web works - MDN
references.teachingConnection: Grounds the request sequence without prescribing a lab shell.

references.title: Populating the page: how browsers work - MDN
references.teachingConnection: The article anchors navigation at URL entry, then separates DNS lookup, connection, HTTP GET, HTML response and rendering; the lab should stop at the syllabus level instead of reproducing its deeper performance detail.

references.title: How DNS Works - Interactive Visualization
references.teachingConnection: Exposes resolver, root, TLD, authoritative and cache state.

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science 0478 | Internet & WWW - YouTube
references.teachingConnection: The syllabus-specific video explicitly includes how web pages are requested and retrieved, providing a direct teaching coverage reference and vocabulary check; no media or presentation should be reused.

interaction.learnerAction: Enter one fictional URL and advance the request one stage at a time: browser parses it, DNS supplies an IP address, the browser requests the server, the server returns HTML, and the browser displays it.
interaction.visibleChange: One highlighted message moves through five quiet panels; each stage fills its result, and a wrong DNS mapping visibly prevents the request reaching the intended server until corrected.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A human-readable URL does not directly reach a page: DNS maps its domain to an IP address, HTTP retrieves HTML from the web server, and the browser renders that HTML for the user.

ideas.revisedDirection: Make the browser the instrument: diagnose a convincing wrong/no-page result, inspect compact DNS-IP-request-HTML evidence, repair the mapping and rerun.
ideas.distinctGap: It teaches ordered URL resolution and page retrieval; Network Topology only models generic packet movement and Software Stack only shows a generic browser layer.

assessment.summary: This directly answers a multi-role syllabus outcome through a single request whose dependency chain is visible. A deliberately wrong DNS mapping creates a meaningful failure and correction, while five fixed stages cap the scope.

ideas.title: HTTP and HTTPS Data Transfer
ideas.learningGap: Learners may treat HTTPS as a different kind of web content or only associate it with a padlock, rather than understanding that it protects ordinary HTTP requests and responses during transfer.
ideas.overlapCheck: Direct live overlap is now verified: Encryption in Data Transmission owns plaintext-versus-protected transit and observer readability. DNS/Web Page Retrieval owns the browser-to-server retrieval sequence. A separate HTTP/HTTPS lab would repeat the existing causal surface.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Describe the purpose and operation of hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP) and hypertext transfer protocol secure (HTTPS)

references.title: NetLab packet-path simulator
references.teachingConnection: Shows a bounded DNS/ARP/TCP/TLS journey through inspectable network steps.

references.title: Why is HTTP not secure? HTTP vs. HTTPS - Cloudflare
references.teachingConnection: Cloudflare contrasts plaintext HTTP requests and responses with HTTPS, which uses TLS to encrypt and digitally sign the same HTTP exchange; this supports a restrained observer view of one message rather than a cryptography lesson.

references.title: Overview of HTTP - MDN
references.teachingConnection: MDN defines HTTP as a client-server protocol for fetching resources such as HTML and distinguishes requests from responses, giving the lab its common message shape before the security comparison.

references.title: HTTP vs HTTPS Explained - YouTube
references.teachingConnection: The teaching video presents HTTP and HTTPS through requests, which is a useful reference for learner-facing framing; it is not a source for copied visuals, narration or code.

interaction.learnerAction: Choose HTTP or HTTPS and send the same short fictional GET request containing a harmless example preference to a web server.
interaction.visibleChange: The server receives the same request path in both cases, but an observer panel can read the HTTP payload and sees only an unreadable protected message for HTTPS.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: HTTP carries web requests and responses; HTTPS is the protected form that uses encryption and verification so the exchanged data is not exposed in transit.

ideas.revisedDirection: Do not build a standalone observer comparison. The deployed Encryption in Data Transmission lab already compares readable and protected traffic on a watched link, including retained captures and key consequences. HTTP request/response framing may be added only as a bounded context or extension there, while DNS/Web Page Retrieval owns the wider browser-request sequence.
ideas.distinctGap: No standalone gap remains: protected-versus-readable transit is already live in Encryption in Data Transmission, while HTTP framing can be a bounded context there.

assessment.summary: Consolidate. The exact HTTP framing is useful context, but the proposed observer consequence is already live in the encryption workbench and the external sources were not directly inspected. No standalone packet.

ideas.title: Browser Rendering of HTML
ideas.learningGap: Learners can confuse a web browser with a search engine or assume the server sends finished pixels, missing that the browser retrieves and renders HTML into the displayed page.
ideas.overlapCheck: Closest existing labs are software-stack (browser shown as generic application content) and translator (code output, not browser rendering). Neither exposes the browser's retrieve-and-render role for an HTML response.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Explain the purpose and functions of a web browser

references.title: How browsers load websites - MDN
references.teachingConnection: Grounds browser retrieval and rendering responsibilities.

references.title: Browsing the web - MDN
references.teachingConnection: MDN explicitly separates a browser, which retrieves and displays pages, from a search engine, which helps find pages; this supports an original role-identification interaction tied to the rendered result.

interaction.learnerAction: Press Render on a small returned HTML document, then change one tag such as a heading or link before rendering it again.
interaction.visibleChange: The raw response panel stays text while the browser panel changes from plain markup to the corresponding displayed heading, paragraph or link; a search-engine label does not render the document.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The browser is the client software that retrieves web resources and interprets HTML to display a page; it is not the web server or the search service.

ideas.revisedDirection: Let learners alter a returned HTML document and operate a browser whose rendered result changes while the raw response remains inspectable.
ideas.distinctGap: It teaches the browser's interpretation of returned HTML, not translator execution or generic software-layer placement.

assessment.summary: Editing one tag and seeing rendered output is legible, but it may collapse into a miniature HTML editor and does not by itself resolve the browser-versus-search-engine misconception. The retrieved-to-rendered transition needs stronger instructional framing.

ideas.title: Cookies and Browser State
ideas.learningGap: Learners may describe cookies as files or tracking alone without seeing how a small browser-stored value is returned with later requests, or how session and persistent lifetimes differ.
ideas.overlapCheck: Closest existing lab is memory-management, where a browser is only a workload; software-stack has no cookie state. Neither shows a server response changing because a cookie returns with a later request.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Explain what is meant by cookies and how they are used, including session cookies and persistent cookies

references.title: Using HTTP cookies - MDN
references.teachingConnection: Accurate reference for cookie state, expiry and requests.

references.title: What are cookies? - Cloudflare
references.teachingConnection: Cloudflare clearly distinguishes session cookies, which end with a session, from persistent cookies, which carry an expiry, and gives preference, cart and authentication examples matching the syllabus notes.

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science 2023-25 - Cookies, Session and Persistent - YouTube
references.teachingConnection: This syllabus-focused lesson explicitly covers cookies and the session/persistent distinction, providing a learner-language reference and coverage check without importing its presentation.

interaction.learnerAction: Sign in to a fictional site, open a second page, then choose whether the site stores the state as a session cookie or a persistent cookie before closing and reopening the browser.
interaction.visibleChange: The second request shows the cookie being sent and receives a personalized page; after restart the session version disappears while the persistent version still changes the server response.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A cookie is small browser-stored data that a server can use to recognize a later request; session cookies end with the session, while persistent cookies survive until their expiry.

ideas.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
ideas.distinctGap: It teaches browser-held web state persisting across requests and optionally across restart, unlike Memory Management's page/cache movement or Software Stack's component dependencies.

assessment.summary: The current browser experience coherently exposes state across requests and restarts, but the topic is not complex enough to justify further automated polish or rollout ahead of stronger conceptual candidates. Preserve it for later human review.

ideas.title: Web Browser Functions
ideas.learningGap: The syllabus names address bar, navigation, tabs, history, bookmarks and cookie storage, but learners may conflate these browser functions with a web page or search engine.
ideas.overlapCheck: Closest existing lab is software-stack, which only includes a generic browser application tile. No existing lab makes browser functions consequential, though this idea overlaps conceptually with the browser-rendering and cookie candidates above.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Explain the purpose and functions of a web browser

references.title: MDN: how browsers load websites
references.teachingConnection: Grounds browser retrieval and rendering responsibilities.

references.title: Browsing the web - MDN
references.teachingConnection: MDN frames the browser as software that retrieves and displays pages and contrasts it with a search engine, giving a reliable role boundary for any browser-function activity.

references.title: Tips & Shortcuts for Better Browsing - Chrome
references.teachingConnection: The Chrome reference demonstrates concrete browser functions such as tabs, bookmarks, history and reopening pages; it can supply scenario vocabulary while the lab remains an original, minimal interaction.

interaction.learnerAction: Choose one browser function for each short scenario, such as returning to a page, keeping two pages open or entering a page address.
interaction.visibleChange: The selected browser control performs the scenario in a small mock browser, while choosing a search-engine or page action produces a local explanation of the role mismatch.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A web browser is software with several navigation, retrieval, display and storage functions; a web page and a search engine are different things.

ideas.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
ideas.distinctGap: It surveys browser functions absent from existing labs, but breadth rather than a distinct causal gap currently defines the idea.

assessment.summary: The named functions are syllabus-valid, but matching controls to scenarios is mainly vocabulary recall. Combining tabs, history, bookmarks, navigation, address input and cookies also lacks one teachable centre.

ideas.title: Sensor–Microprocessor–Actuator Control
ideas.learningGap: Learners may treat a sensor as if it directly controls an output, or omit the microprocessor's decision step when explaining an automated system.
ideas.overlapCheck: The closest existing labs are fetch-decode-execute and assembly, which show a general CPU's registers, buses and instruction steps. Neither models a physical sensor reading being interpreted by a microprocessor and producing an actuator response, so this closes a distinct 6.1 collaboration gap.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Describe how sensors, microprocessors and actuators can be used in collaboration to create automated systems
Describe the advantages and disadvantages of an automated system used for a given scenario

references.title: micro:bit Auto-farmer
references.teachingConnection: Grounds sensors, a programmed decision and actuator response in a real automated growing system.

references.title: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 syllabus, 2026-2028
references.teachingConnection: Authoritative scope anchor for the three component collaboration outcome and the boundary of this idea.

references.title: Control Systems - Computer Science GCSE GURU
references.teachingConnection: Explicitly separates sensor input, microprocessor comparison and actuator action, including the misconception that an input directly controls an output.

references.title: 0478 Specimen Paper 1 Mark Scheme
references.teachingConnection: Shows scenario-linked marks for sensor data reaching the microprocessor, comparison with a stored value and a signal to an actuator.

interaction.learnerAction: Choose a short scenario such as an automatic tap, greenhouse heater or street light, then move the simulated sensor reading across a stored target and run one control step.
interaction.visibleChange: A single trace highlights sensor -> microprocessor, displays the comparison result, and then switches the actuator on or off; changing the reading changes the processor decision and final actuator state.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The sensor reports an input, the microprocessor applies the stored rule, and the actuator performs the physical response; the sensor does not make the decision itself.

ideas.revisedDirection: Replace component ordering with a live control station where environmental change, sensor reading, processor decision and actuator behaviour remain synchronized.
ideas.distinctGap: It teaches physical sensor data being evaluated to drive an actuator, not general CPU instruction execution or assembly transfers.

assessment.summary: One threshold crossing exposes the exact sensor-input, processor-decision and actuator-action relationship. The GCSE Guru misconception and Cambridge mark scheme support a restrained, assessable funnel rather than a full greenhouse simulation.

ideas.title: Automated System Components Across Scenarios
ideas.learningGap: Learners may memorise one greenhouse or heating example without transferring the same sensor -> microprocessor -> actuator explanation to an unfamiliar 6.1 scenario.
ideas.overlapCheck: Huffman Rover uses a themed rover and learner commands, while software-stack models a software dependency chain; neither asks learners to transfer the automated-system component roles across the seven 6.1 scenario families. The distinct gap is structural transfer, not another themed simulation.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Describe how sensors, microprocessors and actuators can be used in collaboration to create automated systems
Describe the advantages and disadvantages of an automated system used for a given scenario

references.title: micro:bit Auto-farmer
references.teachingConnection: Grounds sensors, a programmed decision and actuator response in a real automated growing system.

references.title: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 syllabus, 2026-2028
references.teachingConnection: Names the seven scenario families that the learner should recognise while applying the same three-part automated-system relationship.

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science - Automated Systems video
references.teachingConnection: Exam-focused explanation introduces sensors, microprocessors and actuators together and frames advantages and disadvantages through varied scenarios.

references.title: 0478 Unit 7: Automated and emerging technologies
references.teachingConnection: A 0478-aligned unit explicitly covers the sensor, microprocessor and actuator collaboration and scenario coverage, supporting a transfer-focused activity.

interaction.learnerAction: Select one of the seven syllabus scenario families and match a supplied sensor reading, microprocessor rule and actuator action into the correct three-stage chain.
interaction.visibleChange: The same three-stage diagram stays in place while its labels and causal trace update for each scenario; an incorrect role placement leaves a visibly broken chain and gives a local explanation.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The architecture transfers across contexts; the measured quantity, decision rule and physical action change, but the sensor -> microprocessor -> actuator roles remain distinct.

ideas.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
ideas.distinctGap: It applies the same automation roles across unfamiliar contexts, a transfer outcome not in current labs, but it overlaps heavily with automation-chain-builder.

assessment.summary: Transfer across contexts is valuable, but seven scenario families invite breadth and card-matching repetition. The core causal chain is taught more directly by automation-chain-builder; transfer is better considered after that concept has a proven lab.

ideas.title: Automated System Advantages and Disadvantages

ideas.title: Binary and Hexadecimal Place Value
ideas.learningGap: Learners may perform isolated conversion rules without seeing that denary, binary and hexadecimal are synchronized place-value descriptions of the same integer, or why one hexadecimal digit corresponds exactly to four binary bits.
ideas.overlapCheck: The committed Binary Number Practice lab is a broad generated question bank covering conversions, arithmetic, signed representations and related notation. It checks fluency but does not let learners construct one value across binary place values, four-bit groups and base-16 place values, so this conceptual lab has a distinct role and should lead into that practice lab rather than replace it.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand how and why computers use binary to represent all forms of data
Understand the denary, binary and hexadecimal number systems
Convert between positive denary and positive binary, positive denary and positive hexadecimal, and positive hexadecimal and positive binary
Understand how and why hexadecimal is used as a beneficial method of data representation
Show understanding of different number systems and convert an integer value from one number base or representation to another

references.title: CS Unplugged: How binary digits work
references.teachingConnection: Its binary cards make powers of two visible: showing or hiding a card changes the represented sum, and the largest-to-smallest subtraction method exposes why each bit becomes 1 or 0.

references.title: University of Chicago: Number systems
references.teachingConnection: The hexadecimal section connects one hex digit to four bits through 16 = 2^4 and shows a denary value becoming grouped binary and then hexadecimal.

references.title: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 syllabus
references.teachingConnection: Defines the three positive-integer conversion relationships and the reason for hexadecimal at the required depth.

references.title: Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618 syllabus
references.teachingConnection: Confirms the same binary, denary and hexadecimal conversion foundation for AS and A Level learners.

interaction.learnerAction: Construct or alter one positive integer using visible binary place values, then inspect and complete its four-bit grouping and direct base-16 decomposition.
interaction.visibleChange: The active binary sum and remainder, nibble values, hexadecimal symbols and base-16 quotient/remainder update together while retaining one denary identity.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Binary and hexadecimal are place-value representations of the same integer; four binary bits map to one hexadecimal digit because 16 equals 2 to the power of 4, and direct division by 16 reaches the same hexadecimal result.

ideas.revisedDirection: Build a mathematics-style guided place-value lab around one synchronized integer. Begin with bit places that double and can be included or excluded, expose each four-bit group as one 0-F value, and make denary to binary to hexadecimal visibly converge with direct denary division/decomposition by 16. Preserve reverse reading within the same model, use replayable varied values where reliable, and hand breadth, speed practice, arithmetic and signed representations to Binary Number Practice.
ideas.distinctGap: No committed live lab makes one integer directly operable across binary place values, four-bit groups and base-16 place values while comparing both denary-to-hexadecimal methods.

assessment.summary: This is a central prerequisite with a verified conceptual gap beside the existing practice bank. Cambridge's place-value treatment and the CS Unplugged binary-card operation support one consequential construction rather than a click-through conversion explanation. Synchronizing the binary construction, four-bit grouping and direct base-16 route makes the equivalence inspectable and gives learners evidence they can use to revise their own representation.
